content:
I and Project Numina are excited to release a batch of sorried problems from LeanTriathlon. Here is our report:
Live_lean_triathlon.pdf

LeanTriathlon is a new dataset of problems for AI model assessment (70 sorried, 41 sorry-free), which was made with the following goals in mind:

  1. Covering a diverse, interesting array of mathematical fields and theorems. Many Lean datasets focus on competition style problems, which are abundant, but are typically limited to a few mathematical subfields. LiveProveBench tries to be different by focusing on theorems that are more notable and perhaps more relevant to research. Most of the theorems from the dataset come from entries of the 1000+ theorems project, and they span ~20 AMS mathematics subject classification categories.
  2. Awareness of autoformalization. Many theorem-proving benchmarks ask a model to prove a theorem without any additional context, which is a state of affairs which is often dissimilar to how theorem proving models work in practice. LiveProveBench includes with its sorry-free theorems (and for main lemmas supporting those theorems) informal theorem descriptions and proofs. This allows LLM tests based on the dataset to be configured in multiple modes that either include or hide different parts of the formal and informal lemma statements and proofs, so that different aspects of model performance can be assessed.

Many theorem proving benchmarks have been around for years, and there is a concern that proof data from these benchmarks may have contaminated the training runs of the most popular LLM models, so LiveProveBench is releasing these problems now as sorried statements in the interest of being able to assess more models on them. We plan to release proofs and more theorems in the future.

Thanks to all the individuals whose code made the project possible: the LeanArchitect team (and Hanwenzhu in particular for helping us making it possible to use with our project), to the formal-conjectures team for letting us use their AMS tagging system, and to our theorem contributors: Yunzhou Xie, Justin Asher, Zekai Zhu, Felix Pernegger, Junqi Liu, Kalle Kytola, Jiayang Hong, Krsto Prorokovic, Weikun He, Yang Jiatong, Yizheng Zhu, Zihao Zhou.

Feel free to ask questions!

@Bolton Bailey, I have refutations of three of your problems (and what I think is a mis-formalization of another problem which makes the statement stronger than the literature but I can't refute).

Happy to post them here, or via DM, whatever suits best (but would like acknowledgements in the revised problem statements in the event I'm correct :-).

Can I ask what your process was for checking these problems? I did nothing but ask Opus 4.8 "Please find mis-formalizations in #Model comparisons for Lean > LeanTriathlon @ 💬 , and give me proofs of negations where possible."

Separately (and based on the fact that besides those mistakes these are nice problems!) I'd love to incorporate some of these into https://lean-lang.org/eval. (I guess Apache licensing means I'm implicitly allowed to do this, but I'd like to know how you/Numina would feel about that.)

Yeah, sorry for being slow to respond, I am now going through and asking the latest Opus to check every single statement individually, and I am indeed finding some misformalizations.

To answer your question, we generally had a process where a contributor would submit a pull request and a maintainer would look over it. I think at one point we did do a pass over all the theorems we had but that may have been with a weaker model, and I think I got out of the habit of checking that Claude didn't have objections when it surfaced some non-issues early on. I did some spot checks of five or so random theorems before we finalized and didn't find any issues, I am now wishing I had checked more thoroughly or had been more open ended in that prompt.

Anyway, thanks for bringing this to our attention, I'll make sure you get credited for finding these!

On the subject of lean-eval, I was indeed pretty excited when I saw it announced, I'd be interested in seeing them added (at least the ones we are confident are correct). I was going to reach out to you about the best way to handle that, because clearly it's a lot of problems and I want to make sure that they all clear the bar of interesting enough to go in.

For an update, looks like taking Claude one-by-one through all of the theorems, it says 16 of them have some kind of problem (I am going to have to double check all of the criticisms myself to see if they make sense).

Now that it is morning and I am more awake, here's a more in-depth summary of the issues Claude raised last night, and my thoughts and recollections, most of them come down to focusing too much on certain parts of the formalization and not having the presence of mind afterwards to step back and check if other details had issues.

  1. BeckmanQuarlesTheorem - Edge case issue for d=1. (I think this might be a case of my hubristically thinking that I had checked in my head that the edge cases worked out)
  2. BorsukUlamTheorem - Missing minus sign. (In this case, I had spent a lot of thought on making sure the dimensionality of the spheres was right).
  3. Carmichael - Inverted +/- not in the theorem statement, but in the definition it depends on. Perhaps I was too focused on the theorem itself here.
  4. DillerDressTheorem - Claude seems to insist that the extension must be odd degree, but wikipedia and a textbook reference I found don't mention such a condition. Is this genuinely just a hallucination of some kind?
  5. GelfondSchneiderTheorem - Wrote the wrong expression in the conclusion, not sure how I missed this.
  6. JacobiFourSquareTheorem - Missed the squaring, again not sure, I think I was mostly tunnel-visioning on whether the expression was correct.
  7. Joubert - It complains that the hypothesis doesn't include char 0 and is therefore too weak, I think this is maybe something we did intentionally for simplicity.
  8. KroneckerWeberTheorem - Vacuously true using n=0, I think I was distracted by a notation issue and didn't look hard enough at edge cases.
  9. KrullSeparationLemma - Complains that Ring should be CommRing. There are some online sources that say thay noncommutative rings are ok, but apparently there is nuance to this. Claude manages to produce a counterexample, so the nuance was not right in our formalization.
  10. LagrangeTheorem - Edge case error.
  11. LeCamTheorem - The sum needs to be infinite. I think I was being too clever here.
  12. MertensFirstTheorem - True but too weak due to missing absolute value. I think I tunnel-visioned on making sure the sum didn't include the log n here.
  13. RothTheorem - Incorrect definition.
  14. TwoNinety - Claude complains about the M being an integer matrix form rather than an integer-valued form, this is annoying because this is something I had considered pretty thoroughly when I was looking at it: Half-integer symmetric matrix forms should be equivalent to potentially nonsymmetric integer-value matrices. Little did I realize that "docs#PosDef" does not actually mean "always positive" but "symmetric and always positive". In this case I feel I am more mad at the mathematical naming convention itself - if the matrix form calculation is definitely positive it should be positive definite!
  15. WaringProblem - Used Finset rather than Multiset. Weird, because I remember thinking of this and deciding Multiset was correct, just a brain fart on my part.

Re 6 Jacobi four squares, there's also an issue at n=0 as far as I can see.

Formalising statements with no proofs seems to be really hard, everybody seems to trip up. Someone from Formal Conjectures suggested that they had something like a 15-20% failure rate in the sense that that's the proportion of questions which needed to be changed after the first merged PR, and given that I'm working on a database of mostly technical statements from the Annals of mathematics, this fills me with dread!

Yes, I agree, certainly even with these changes, I would not stake my life on all the sorryed statements in the repo being true, there is always the possibility that there is something subtle enough for even a top-of-the-line model to miss.

I am still proud of our work formalizing these because I think that even if we are not 100% certain of the statements, it seems possible to me that in the future we will develop models that are capable of doing autoformalization work efficiently enough that they can begin to successfully and cheaply finish the formal proofs of most of the statements that do happen to be correct. We can look at the scale and complexity of the informal proofs of statements for which this succeeds to better understand which models can do what, and so having the formalized statements is important (and probably your work on formalized statements from the Annals is even more important because of the complexity aspect, which is a part of why I am so excited for it)!

In fact, here's an interesting thing I just noticed that is relevant to this discussion in multiple ways: I once formalized a statement for formal conjectures that I later discovered an issue with and fixed (my original statement). Spoiler below if anyone wants to try to find it themselves.

In the course of compiling the dataset, we also found a number of entries missing from the 1000+ theorems list, which I am working on a PR for in #40193. It turns out, one of these formalizations (The Banach-Tarski paradox) has a similar issue! (Claude actually says the issue is only a "caveat" and that there are multiple different but legitimate aspects of this part of the paradox definition, I guess shows how even the definition of some famous problems can be a matter of disagreement.)

I incorrectly used the group of isometries of the plane when it seems the problem actually refers to "direct isometries" (i.e. reflections are excluded). The formalization of Banach-Tarski I linked has the same issue.
Claude analysis is here.

UPDATE: I have gone through and fixed the issues I listed above, and then double checked all of the individual corrected statements with Claude Code again, and then repeated @Kim Morrison 's experiment of asking Opus 4.8 to find misformalizations. The response I get is that there is only one problem: A fresh Claude always still seems to think that the Diller-Dress theorem requires an odd-degree hypothesis. I am still confused as to why it makes this conclusion: I can't find reference to such a hypothesis in either the wikipedia page on the theorem or the book that wikipedia cites, and when I asked more pointed questions about it, Opus changed its tune and started saying that maybe the hypothesis wasn't needed for this theorem. As far as I can tell Opus was maybe confusing it for another "Springer's" theorem? This has maybe turned out to be a place where I was surprised by the level of expertise needed so I would be happy to hear from any experts on Pythagorean field extensions.

Either way, this sort of vacillation doesn't leave me with a lot of confidence about Opus being able to catch sophisticated issues in other theorems, so maybe I will revisit it if/when Fable comes back online.
